lessons.title: The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths

before.exam_tip_html: For questions on this topic, examiners reward the use of accurate Pali terminology. Use the Pali register throughout: dukkha, tanhā, nirodha, magga, dhamma, kamma, nibbāna. You may gloss the Sanskrit equivalent once (e.g. ‘nibbāna, or nirvāna in Sanskrit’), but mixing Pali and Sanskrit in the same answer suggests confusion about the tradition. For an 8-mark ‘explain two beliefs’ question on suffering, pick two of the Four Noble Truths and explain each with its Pali name, its meaning, and why it matters — always link to the Dhammapada or the Deer Park Sermon as a source of authority.
before.content_html:
Who Was the Buddha?

The word ‘Buddha’ is not a personal name but a title meaning ‘the awakened one’ or ‘the enlightened one.’ The person to whom it refers was Siddhattha Gotama (Sanskrit: Siddhartha Gautama), a prince born into the Shakya clan in what is now southern Nepal, traditionally dated to around the 5th–4th century BCE. According to the tradition preserved in the Pali texts, Siddhattha’s birth was accompanied by predictions that he would become either a great king or a great spiritual teacher.

His father, wishing Siddhattha to become a king, raised him in great luxury within a palace, shielding him from anything unpleasant. Siddhattha married, had a son, and seemed set for a life of privilege — yet the tradition records that he remained inwardly unsatisfied. The turning point came when he ventured outside the palace grounds.

The Four Sights

According to the tradition, Siddhattha encountered four sights on separate journeys outside the palace that transformed his understanding of life. The Four Sights were:

  • An old person — stooped and frail, showing Siddhattha that youth is temporary and all beings are subject to ageing.
  • A sick person — suffering from illness, revealing that physical wellbeing cannot be relied upon.
  • A corpse — showing directly that death is unavoidable for every living being.
  • A wandering holy man (a samana) — a spiritual seeker who had renounced ordinary life to pursue liberation from suffering. Unlike the first three sights, this one offered possibility: perhaps there was a way beyond the suffering that the other three had revealed.
Key Fact

The Four Sights are: old age, sickness, death, and a holy man. The first three showed Siddhattha the reality of suffering; the fourth showed him that liberation might be possible through the spiritual life.

Renunciation and the Ascetic Life

Siddhattha left his palace, his wife and his young son in the middle of the night — an act of renunciation. He became a wandering ascetic, practising severe self-denial — eating almost nothing, exposing his body to extremes of heat and cold — to see whether physical mortification could bring liberation. After years of this ‘ascetic’ life, he concluded that it was as far from the truth as his earlier life of luxury had been. Neither extreme led to freedom. This insight led him to formulate what Buddhism calls the Middle Way — a path that avoids both excess and harsh deprivation.

Enlightenment

Siddhattha sat in deep meditation beneath a pipal tree (later called the Bodhi tree, ‘tree of awakening’) at Bodh Gaya and resolved not to rise until he had understood the true nature of existence. Through the night he achieved Enlightenment — seeing the world ‘as it really is.’ He understood the nature of suffering, its cause, its end, and the path that leads to its end. At this point Siddhattha became the Buddha: the awakened one.

The Deer Park Sermon: First Turning of the Wheel

After his enlightenment the Buddha travelled to Isipatana (near present-day Varanasi, India) where he found five former companions in the Deer Park. There he delivered his first teaching — an event known as the ‘first turning of the wheel of dhamma’. In this sermon the Buddha set out what would become the core of Buddhist teaching: the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. The Deer Park Sermon marks the beginning of the Buddhist community (the sangha) and the first communication of the dhamma to others.

The Four Noble Truths are structured like a medical diagnosis: identify the illness, find its cause, confirm that a cure exists, and prescribe the treatment.

1. Dukkha — the truth of suffering. Dukkha is often translated as ‘suffering’, but the Pali word is richer than this. It encompasses obvious suffering (pain, grief, illness) but also the deeper dissatisfaction that arises from impermanence: pleasures do not last; relationships end; even joy carries the shadow of its own passing. The Dhammapada, verse 1 (Pali: Manopubbangama dhamma…) teaches that mental states precede all actions, meaning that suffering is rooted in the mind as much as in external circumstances. The Buddha is not a pessimist — he acknowledges joy — but insists that clinging to things that are impermanent creates suffering.

2. Samudaya — the cause of suffering. The cause of dukkha is tanhā (craving or thirst). There are three types: craving for sensory pleasure, craving for existence (clinging to life), and craving for non-existence (wishing for annihilation). The Dhammapada, verse 5, reinforces this with the teaching that hatred (a form of craving) is not overcome by hatred but by its opposite. Tanhā drives the cycle of rebirth (samsāra) because unfulfilled craving leads to further becoming.

3. Nirodha — the cessation of suffering. Nirodha means cessation — the total letting go of tanhā. When craving is extinguished, the conditions for suffering are removed. This state of complete liberation is nibbāna (Sanskrit: nirvāna) — not a place but an experience of freedom from craving, hatred and delusion. The Buddha himself is the proof that nirodha is possible, not merely a theoretical ideal.

4. Magga — the path. Magga is the path to nirodha: the Noble Eightfold Path. The Buddha is presenting not just a diagnosis but a practical programme for living.

Key Fact

The Four Noble Truths in Pali are: Dukkha (suffering/dissatisfaction), Samudaya (craving/tanhā as the cause), Nirodha (cessation — the end of craving is possible), and Magga (the Eightfold Path as the way to nirodha). This structure mirrors a medical diagnosis and treatment.

The Noble Eightfold Path: Three Sections

The Eightfold Path is not eight sequential steps but eight interrelated practices grouped into three sections. All three sections are cultivated together.

Wisdom (paññā) — right understanding (understanding the Four Noble Truths and the nature of reality) and right intention (committing to renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness rather than craving, ill-will and cruelty).

Morality (sīla) — right speech (avoiding lying, harsh speech, gossip), right action (avoiding killing, stealing, sexual misconduct), and right livelihood (not earning a living through harmful means).

Meditation (samādhi) — right effort (cultivating positive states of mind and abandoning negative ones), right mindfulness (clear, present-moment awareness of body, feelings, mind and mental objects), and right concentration (developing the deep stillness of meditation, the jhānas).

Living by the Eightfold Path is the Buddhist way of progressively loosening the grip of tanhā until craving is extinguished and nibbāna is attained. The Buddha presented this not as a set of commandments from a divine authority but as a map tested through his own experience. The invitation is to try the path and see for oneself whether it works.

lessons.title: Meditation, the Three Marks and the Three Jewels

before.content_html:
The Three Marks of Existence

The Buddha taught that all conditioned phenomena share three fundamental characteristics, known in Pali as the Three Marks of Existence (tilakkhaṇa). Understanding these marks is central to Buddhist practice because ignorance of them is, according to the dhamma, the root cause of continued suffering. The Three Marks are: anicca (impermanence), dukkha (suffering / dissatisfaction) and anatta (no fixed self).

Key Fact

The Three Marks of Existence are: anicca (impermanence — nothing lasts), dukkha (suffering / dissatisfaction — unsatisfactoriness runs through all conditioned life) and anatta (no fixed self — there is no permanent, unchanging soul). These are Pali terms from the Theravāda tradition.

Anicca: Impermanence

Anicca teaches that everything changes. Feelings, thoughts, relationships, physical bodies and the entire material world are in a constant state of flux. Nothing that exists in the conditioned world stays the same from one moment to the next. The Buddha is recorded in the dhamma as teaching that clinging to things as if they were permanent is the source of much suffering: because we treat impermanent things as if they will last, we suffer when they change or end. Recognising anicca — truly internalising it rather than just accepting it intellectually — is a step toward liberation.

Anatta and the Story of Nagasena

Anatta is perhaps the most philosophically distinctive of the Three Marks. It teaches that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul. This differs from Hindu teaching (which speaks of an eternal atman) and from popular conceptions of the self as a fixed entity that persists through time. The Story of Nagasena (from the Milindapanha text) has the monk Nagasena explain anatta to King Milinda using the analogy of a chariot. He asks: where is the chariot? Is it the wheels? The axle? The frame? None of the individual parts is “the chariot”, and neither is the sum of them — the chariot is merely a convenient label. In the same way, “I” am not any of the aggregates (khandas) that make up experience.

Dhammapada 113 connects anatta and the aggregates. Without citing this verse’s exact phrasing (to avoid fabrication), its context affirms that a moment of insight into the impermanent, selfless nature of existence is of greater value than a long life lived in ignorance. This supports the Buddhist emphasis on wisdom (paññā) as essential to liberation.

Buddhist teaching identifies five aggregates (khandas) that together constitute what we call a person: rūpa (form or body), vedanā (sensation / feeling), saññā (perception), sankhāra (mental formations / volitional activities) and viññāṇa (consciousness). None of these is permanent, and none of them, individually or combined, constitutes a fixed self. This “bundle” view of personal identity supports the teaching of anatta: what we call “me” is a constantly changing process, not a fixed thing.

The Three Jewels: Taking Refuge

At the heart of Buddhist identity is the act of taking refuge in the Three Jewels (tiratana): the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. To “take refuge” means to commit one’s life to these three sources of guidance. The formula repeated by Buddhists is: “I take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dhamma; I take refuge in the Sangha.”

Each jewel has a distinct role. The Buddha is the example of an enlightened being — he shows that liberation (nibbāna) is achievable by a human being. The Dhamma is the path and the teachings that guide practitioners toward liberation. The Sangha is the community of practitioners — including monks, nuns and lay people — who support one another and keep the teachings alive across generations. In Theravāda Buddhism, the Sangha primarily refers to those who have attained one of the stages of enlightenment; in broader usage it includes all Buddhist communities worldwide.

Key Fact

The Three Jewels (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) are the foundation of Buddhist identity and practice. Taking refuge in them is the formal act of becoming a Buddhist and commits the practitioner to a life guided by the Buddha’s example, the dhamma’s wisdom and the Sangha’s community.

Meditation: Samatha

Samatha meditation (calm / tranquillity meditation) develops concentration and stillness of mind. In the most common form, the meditator focuses attention on the natural rhythm of the breath. When the mind wanders — which it inevitably does — the meditator gently returns attention to the breath without judgement. Over time, this practice builds the mental stability (samādhi) needed for deeper insight. The Dhammapada verse 282 teaches that wisdom arises through meditation and that without meditation, wisdom is lost — affirming the central place of meditative practice in the path to liberation.

Meditation: Mettābhāvanā

Mettābhāvanā (loving-kindness meditation) systematically develops goodwill and compassion. The practitioner begins by generating warm feelings toward themselves, then extends those feelings outward — to loved ones, to neutral people, to people they find difficult, and finally to all living beings without exception. The goal is to break down the mental barriers between “self” and “other”, which accords with the teaching of anatta. Mettābhāvanā is closely linked to the quality of mettā (loving-kindness), one of the four brahmavihāras (divine abodes) taught in the Theravāda tradition.

Vipassanā meditation (insight meditation) involves closely observing mental and physical experiences as they arise and pass away. Rather than fixing attention on one object (as in samatha), vipassanā trains the meditator to notice the impermanent, unsatisfying and selfless nature of all experience directly — not just as a concept but as a lived reality. This direct insight into the Three Marks is considered, in Theravāda teaching, the proximate cause of enlightenment. Samatha and vipassanā are often practised together: samatha builds the mental stability required for vipassanā to arise.

In contemporary Britain, Buddhist retreat centres offer residential meditation courses in both samatha and vipassanā traditions. The Lam Rim Buddhist Centre is a well-known British retreat offering intensive residential practice across meditation traditions.
before.exam_tip_html: When writing about the Three Marks of Existence, always use the correct Pali terms: anicca, dukkha, anatta. Mixing Pali and Sanskrit terms (e.g. writing ‘nirvana’ in a Theravāda-focused answer) will signal weak understanding to the examiner. For 8-mark ‘Explain two beliefs’ questions, ensure each belief is developed with an explanation of its significance — not just a definition — and link to a source such as the Dhammapada or the Story of Nagasena. For evaluation questions, consider non-Buddhist views on the concept of self or the value of meditation for wellbeing.

lessons.title: Ethical Behaviour, Festivals and Sangha Practice

before.content_html:
The Five Precepts

Buddhist ethical life is guided by the Five Precepts (pañcasila). These are voluntary commitments, not commandments imposed by an external authority. Dhammapada 183 describes the teaching of the Buddhas as: not to do evil, to cultivate good and to purify the mind. The Five Precepts operationalise this in daily life.

The Five Precepts are: (1) not harming any living being; (2) not taking what has not been given; (3) avoiding sexual misconduct; (4) avoiding false speech; (5) abstaining from substances that cloud the mind. Together they reflect the Buddhist commitment to sīla (morality), which alongside wisdom (paññā) and meditation (samādhi) forms the three sections of the Eightfold Path.

The first precept — ahimsa (non-harming) — has wide implications. Many Buddhists adopt a vegetarian or vegan diet as a natural expression of not harming animals. Career choices may also be affected: a committed Buddhist following the first precept might avoid occupations involving weapons manufacture, slaughterhouse work or pest control.

The third precept (avoiding sexual misconduct) requires interpreting what “misconduct” means. For monastics, celibacy is the standard. For lay practitioners, it means avoiding relationships that cause harm to oneself or others — such as infidelity or relationships with those unable to freely consent. The fifth precept (avoiding intoxicants) has implications for social life: alcohol and recreational drugs cloud the mind, making clear perception and ethical action more difficult.

Challenges for Triratna Buddhists (the British-based movement formerly known as the Western Buddhist Order) are particularly interesting. Living according to the Five Precepts in a Western consumer culture — where alcohol is normalised, meat-eating is common and sexual permissiveness is widespread — presents a daily counter-cultural challenge. Triratna communities emphasise communal support and regular retreat as ways to maintain ethical practice.

Places of Practice: Vihara and Home Shrine

A vihara (monastery / place of practice) is the traditional centre of Buddhist communal life. It houses monks or nuns who follow the Vinaya (monastic code), practise daily meditation and provide teaching for lay Buddhists. Lay people visit viharas for teachings, meditation sessions and festivals. The vihara also preserves the Pali texts of the Theravāda tradition.

Many Buddhist households maintain a home shrine as a focus for daily practice. A typical home shrine contains an image of the Buddha (as a focus for reflection, not as an object of worship in the sense of prayer to a deity), candles representing the light of the dhamma, incense representing the spread of good qualities, flowers representing impermanence, and water offerings. Daily bowing and the recitation of the refuges (“I take refuge in the Buddha...”) before the shrine maintains mindfulness and devotion throughout ordinary life.

Key Fact

Theravāda puja typically venerates a single image of the historical Buddha (Siddhattha Gotama). Mahāyāna puja may venerate multiple Buddhas, bodhisattvas and use mudras (hand gestures), mantras (sacred sounds) and mandalas (sacred diagrams) as part of elaborate ritual practice.

Theravāda and Mahāyāna Puja

Theravāda puja is relatively austere. A single image of the historical Buddha is honoured through offerings (flowers, incense, water, light). The act is understood as an expression of reverence and aspiration — not as petitionary prayer. The shrine reminds the practitioner of the qualities of the enlightened mind that they are cultivating.

Mahāyāna puja is typically more elaborate. It may incorporate veneration of multiple Buddhas (such as Amida Buddha, associated with Pure Land Buddhism) and bodhisattvas (beings who delay their own final liberation to assist all sentient beings). Ritual elements include mudras (symbolic hand gestures), mantras (sacred sounds or phrases repeated as part of devotion) and mandalas (intricate sacred diagrams used as visual meditation objects). Dana (giving) is central to both traditions: lay people offer food to monks and monasteries, generating merit and supporting the monastic community.

Wesak

Wesak is the most widely celebrated Buddhist festival, observed at the full moon of May. For Theravāda Buddhists, Wesak commemorates all three of the most significant events in the Buddha’s life: his birth, his enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and his death (parınibbāna). For Mahāyāna Buddhists, these events are commemorated separately at different times of year.

Wesak celebrations include visiting viharas, making offerings, listening to dhamma teachings, releasing caged birds (symbolising liberation), lantern processions and acts of generosity. The festival reinforces the central Buddhist narrative — that a human being (Siddhattha Gotama) achieved enlightenment through effort and practice, and that this achievement is available to all.

Kathina is a festival of robe-offering that marks the end of Vassa — the traditional three-month rainy-season retreat for Theravāda monastics. During Vassa, monks remain in one location, practise intensively and do not travel. At Kathina (held in October / November), lay supporters bring new robes and supplies to the monasteries as an act of dana. This mutual relationship — monastics offering dhamma teaching and ethical example, lay people offering material support — expresses the interdependence of the Sangha.

Parinirvana Day (observed in February in Mahāyāna traditions) marks the Buddha’s death and his passing into final nibbāna — the complete cessation of the cycle of rebirth. It is observed with meditation, readings from the Buddhist texts and reflection on impermanence — the very teaching the Buddha exemplified by dying.

Key Fact

Three key Buddhist festivals: Wesak (birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha — for Theravāda), Kathina (robe-offering, end of monks’ Vassa retreat) and Parinirvana Day (Buddha’s final death, observed in Mahāyāna traditions in February).

glossary_terms.definition: The five ethical guidelines for Buddhist lay practitioners: not harming, not taking what is not given, avoiding sexual misconduct, avoiding false speech, and not taking intoxicants.
The Pali term for morality or ethical conduct — one of the three sections of the Eightfold Path alongside wisdom (panna) and meditation (samadhi).
Non-harming: the principle of not causing harm to any living being, which has implications for diet, career, lifestyle and relationships in Buddhist practice.

A modern British-based Buddhist movement (formerly known as the Western Buddhist Order), practising across Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions, which encourages lay practitioners to live according to the Five Precepts.
A Buddhist monastery or place of practice where monks and nuns live, meditate and keep the dhamma alive; also used for lay meditation centres.
Theravada Buddhism: the 'teaching of the elders', practised mainly in South and South-East Asia, which closely follows the Pali canon and emphasises individual liberation through the Eightfold Path.
Mahayana Buddhism: the 'great vehicle', widespread in East Asia, which extends the Buddhist path to include the bodhisattva ideal of seeking enlightenment for the benefit of all beings.
In Mahayana Buddhism, enlightened beings who delay their own final liberation in order to help all other sentient beings reach enlightenment.
Ritual offerings and acts of devotion in Buddhist practice, carried out before a shrine or image as an expression of reverence, aspiration and gratitude.
The most important Buddhist festival, celebrating the birth of the Buddha (and, in Theravada tradition, also his enlightenment and death), observed at the full moon of May.
The Buddhist festival of robe-offering, celebrated at the end of Vassa (the monks' rainy-season retreat), when lay people present new robes and supplies to the monastic Sangha.
The traditional three-month retreat observed by Theravada Buddhist monks during the rainy season, during which they remain in one place to practise intensively.

before.exam_tip_html: For ‘Describe’ and ‘Explain’ questions on Buddhist practice, use correct Pali terminology consistently (sīla for morality, paññā for wisdom, samādhi for meditation, dana for giving) — this demonstrates the depth of understanding examiners reward. When comparing Theravāda and Mahāyāna puja, name specific differences (e.g. bodhisattvas in Mahāyāna, mudras and mantras). For 15-mark evaluations, consider both Buddhist and non-religious perspectives on ethical guidelines — for example, how a Humanist would judge the Five Precepts compared to a Theravāda Buddhist.
